items.correction: The core holds and the fix works. One detail was wrong: the reviewer wrote that a plain .xml score 'replaces the player in the tab'. Chrome and Edge (since version 85) open a dropped file that no page code accepts in a NEW tab, so the player stays on screen but never receives the file. This review's own spike saw exactly that: the .xml file opened in a new tab, and Punk.gp gave a new blank tab. Firefox and Safari were not tested (untested); they may still open the file in place of the player. The other detail holds: 'Drop to open' disappeared the moment the drag crossed onto the card.

items.central_claim_check: Read web/app/play/PlayerShell.tsx. The drop handlers sit on the drop-zone <section> only: onDragEnter (:1046), onDragLeave (:1051), onDragOver (:1055) and onDrop (:1064). The only window-level listeners are dragend and pointermove (:957-967), and they only end the 'dragging' state; nothing cancels dragover or drop at window or document level. A search of web/app, web/lib and client/src finds no other dragover or drop handler. web/app/layout.tsx:15-27 renders the page and then the Toaster inside <body>, so a card rendered there is a sibling of the player's <main>, outside the drop zone. The comment beside the drop overlay (PlayerShell.tsx:1109-1113) records the same trap: an overlay mounted outside the container broke the drag counter, because 'every dragleave's relatedTarget was the overlay, which is not a descendant'. MDN's File drag and drop guide (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTML_Drag_and_Drop_API/File_drag_and_drop) says the browser may open or download a dropped file that no drop target accepts. Chromium change 8bee828 (https://crrev.com/8bee82851b8e9bc7ab7f049194ad259743db2c97), shipped in Chrome 85, makes such a drop open in a new tab instead of replacing the page. The existing drop test (web/e2e/player.e2e.ts:348) will run in Sydney once the config sets that time zone (section 1), so it never meets the card.
items.contradicts: none — checked section 3 (Where, Non-blocking, Answering), section 1 (layout.tsx renders the card), section 9 (the No overlap case) and G7. pointer-events: none during a file drag changes nothing for clicks or the keyboard, and the card stays visible.

spike.what: A one-page copy of the player's drop-zone shape: a section with the same depth counter and the same dragenter, dragleave, dragover and drop handlers, an overlay inside it, and a fixed card rendered OUTSIDE it, the way layout.tsx would render the popup. Real file drags were driven through Chrome's own drag pipeline (the Chrome DevTools Protocol's Input.dispatchDragEvent, copy-only source), the way web/e2e/player.e2e.ts drives its drop test, in headless Chromium from the Playwright 1.61.1 already in web/node_modules. Five runs: today's design with 1-beat.musicxml and with Punk.gp; a control drop on the score; the fix with the drag entering over the score; the fix with the card as the drag's first contact. The After text was applied to a scratch copy of the spec together with Group C's other Afters; the repo's own Prettier (print width 100), markdownlint-cli2 and cspell all pass on it.
spike.result: Today's design: the drop-zone handler never ran (events seen: zone dragenter, card dragenter, zone dragleave; no drop). 'Drop to open' went from shown to hidden as the drag crossed onto the card. Chromium opened 1-beat.musicxml in a new tab and gave Punk.gp a new blank tab; the player's own page did not change. Control: a drop on the score reached the handler. With the fix, both runs reached the handler (Punk.gp received), 'Drop to open' stayed visible over the card, no new tab opened, and the fix switched itself off on the drop. A real file drop in Firefox or Safari was not tested (untested).

items.scenario: You open the player in Berlin. The privacy question waits at the bottom of the screen, over the lower part of the score. You drag your song 'Punk.gp' from the desktop towards the score. As you pass over the question box, 'Drop to open' disappears. You let go there anyway. The player does not open your song: Chrome opens a new tab with nothing useful in it, and the player still shows the old beat. Other browsers may replace the player with the file (not tested).
items.whats_wrong: The popup is rendered by web/app/layout.tsx, so it is not inside the player's drop zone. The drop zone accepts a drop only on itself and on the elements inside it, and nothing else on the page accepts one. A file dropped on the card therefore never reaches the player, and the browser handles the file itself (it opens or downloads it). Section 3 promises 'The player works while the card waits', and no case in section 9 drops a file on the card. The existing drop test runs in Sydney, where the card never shows.

items.proposed_fix: Add one bullet to section 3: while a file is dragged over the page, the card has pointer-events: none, so a drop on the card lands in the player's drop zone. A dragenter on the window that carries files starts it; the drop, dragend or the next pointermove ends it. Add one end-to-end case in Berlin that drops a real file on the card and expects it to open, with no new tab, and name that case in section 1's row for privacy-choice.e2e.ts.
items.why_it_works: With pointer-events: none the browser looks straight through the card, so every drag event lands on the score or the transport row underneath. Both are inside the drop zone, and its existing handlers accept the drop. The switch listens on the window, not on the drop zone, so it also works when the card is the first thing the drag touches (spiked). A switch tied to the drop zone's own 'dragging' state would never start in that case, because the drop zone never sees the drag. The end-of-drag signals PlayerShell already trusts switch it back, so the card can be clicked again at once.

plain_terms.drop zone: the part of the player that accepts a dropped file: the score area, the left rail and the transport row
plain_terms.pointer-events: none: a CSS setting that makes the mouse, and a drag, pass through an element to whatever is underneath
plain_terms.dragenter / dragend / pointermove: browser events: a drag reaches an element; a drag ends; the mouse moves (it does not fire during a drag)
plain_terms.Chrome DevTools Protocol: the control channel the end-to-end tests use to drive a real drag inside Chrome
plain_terms.G7: decision G7: the popup is built in this ticket, as a floating card above the player's controls

items.correction: One reason was overstated. An element can be a labelled region and also carry aria-live; nothing forbids both. The real problem is timing: the card arrives together with its text, and MDN's live-region guide says screen readers generally announce only changes to a live region that already exists (and that this varies between browsers and screen readers). So if the card itself is the live region, 'announced politely when it appears' will usually not happen. The fix is unchanged.

items.central_claim_check: web/app/play/PlayerShell.tsx:1235-1242 keeps an always-mounted, visually hidden paragraph with aria-live="polite". Its comment says: 'a live region added to the DOM at the same moment its text appears is not announced at all — the region has to be there first.' MDN's ARIA live regions guide (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Guides/Live_regions) gives the same advice: create the region empty first, change its text later, and put it in the page's first HTML for the most reliable result. The card can only appear after hydration (spec line 445), because the time zone and the saved answer are known only in the browser. MDN notes one exception: role="alert" is usually announced even when it is inserted with its text, but it interrupts the screen reader, is often read with the word 'Alert' first, and is meant for urgent messages, so it does not fit a polite question.
items.contradicts: none — checked section 3 (Screen readers, Non-blocking), section 9 (the PrivacyChoices unit tests and the axe scan with the popup open), 'To verify at plan time' (no layout shift: a visually hidden region takes no space) and section 2's rule that nothing shows when neither key is set (an empty, silent region shows nothing).

spike.why: Whether speech happens needs a real screen reader (VoiceOver or NVDA) and a person listening; a headless browser cannot tell. The behaviour is stated by the repo's own comment and by MDN. items.scenario: You use a screen reader and open Notation Hero in Berlin. A moment after the page loads, a privacy question appears at the bottom of the screen. items.whats_wrong: Section 3 says the card is 'announced politely when it appears'. The obvious way to build that is aria-live on the card itself. But the card is added to the page together with its text, after hydration, and a live region that arrives with its text is generally not announced. The repo met this before in PlayerShell.tsx and solved it with an empty live region that stays on the page. Neither the unit tests nor the axe scan in section 9 would notice the silence.

items.why_it_works: The region is on the page, empty, from the first paint. When the card appears, its question arrives as a change to a live region that already exists, which is the case screen readers announce. It is the pattern PlayerShell.tsx already uses for 'Opened …' and for a failed open, so there is nothing new to invent.

plain_terms.live region: a part of the page that a screen reader reads out when its text changes, without the person moving to it
plain_terms.polite: the screen reader waits for a pause instead of interrupting
plain_terms.hydration: the moment the page's code starts running in the browser, after the first HTML has arrived
plain_terms.labelled region: a named area of the page ('Privacy choice') that screen-reader users can jump to
plain_terms.axe: the automated accessibility checker used in the web job
plain_terms.role=\"alert\": a live region for urgent messages, read out at once, interrupting the screen reader

items.central_claim_check: Read the 2026-10-05 spike (throwaway, not in the repo). Its instrumentation-client.ts queued gtag('consent', 'default', {…}) and then gtag('set', { allow_google_signals: false, allow_ad_personalization_signals: false }): a separate settings step. Its js and config calls came from @next/third-parties 16.3.6's GoogleAnalytics component, whose inline script calls gtag('js', new Date()) and then gtag('config', <ID>) with no settings object (checked in the published package, https://unpkg.com/@next/third-parties@16.3.6/dist/google/ga.js). So the queue the spike ran was consent, set, js, then config with only the ID. The spec's sketch (lines 182-193) has no set step and puts the two settings inside config, a shape the spike never ran. Google's privacy-controls guide (https://developers.google.com/tag-platform/security/guides/privacy) documents both places for these two settings (set for every tag on the page, config for one property), so the sketch is not wrong, only unverified while the spec calls it verified.

items.proposed_fix: Make mixer_change a union on control: the six one-track controls (render, solo, mute, transpose_audio, transpose_full, staff) carry instrument; solo_all, mute_all and layout carry only on. Name the one-track twin trackInstrument(), make the ✅ example call it, add a ✅ example for Solo all, say in the paragraph which controls carry no instrument, and add trackInstrument() to section 1's score-facts.ts row. In the example the track is called leadGuitar, not track: at a real call site, a variable named track would hide the track() function.

Naming trackInstrument() gives the brand its one legal maker, so 'a free string never type-checks' holds and the ✅ example is a real call.

plain_terms.branded string: a text type that only one function may create, so ordinary text cannot be passed where it is expected
plain_terms.union on control: the event has two allowed shapes, and the value of control decides which one applies
plain_terms.tsc: the TypeScript compiler, run here only to check types
plain_terms.instrumentsValue(): the function from the Sentry spec (PR #191) that turns a score's tracks into a value such as drums,025,033
plain_terms.trackInstrument(): the proposed one-track version: drums, or one track's General MIDI program in three digits, such as 025
plain_terms.@ts-expect-error: a comment that tells TypeScript the next line must fail to compile; if it compiles, the check fails

track('mixer_change', { control: 'solo', on: true, track: 'Lead Guitar' });

items.central_claim_check: Spiked with TypeScript 5.9.3 (tsc --strict). TypeScript checks for extra keys only on an object written directly inside the call. A fields object built first, merged in with a spread, or returned by a helper, each also carrying a track name, compiled with no error. Section 4 (line 203) says track() sends gtag('event', name, fields), and section 9 (line 375) tests for ['event', name, fields], so the object goes to Google as given. The privacy end-to-end case (lines 388-389) opens a file and checks Google's requests, but presses no mixer control, so it cannot see a name sent by a control.
items.contradicts: none — checked section 4 (the track() bullet), section 5 (the promise on lines 220-221), section 9 (the track() unit test, the Types test, the Privacy case) and 'Extending later' (a second sender inside track(): the copy happens before any sender, so a second sender gets the same clean fields).

spike.what: (c) A scratch .ts file type-checked with tsc --strict: the same track() signature, and mixer_change calls whose fields carry a track name in five ways. Then the proposed fix in a second file: a per-event key list that tsc checks against AnalyticsEvents in both directions, and a track() that copies only the listed keys. It was type-checked, run with Node 24, and type-checked again with two broken key lists. The After text was applied to a scratch copy of the spec together with Group C's other Afters; the repo's own Prettier (print width 100), markdownlint-cli2 and cspell all pass on it.
spike.result: Only the object written inside the call is rejected. Built first, spread in, returned by a helper, and the whole-mixer shape built first with an extra key: all four compile. With the fix, the built-first object still compiles, but what reaches the queue is control, on and instrument only; the track name is gone. tsc rejects a key list that misses a declared field, and one that names a key the event does not declare.

items.scenario: You open your own song file in Sydney and solo the track called 'Lead Guitar'. Months later, a change builds that event's fields in a small helper that also keeps the track's name for another use. It still compiles, and 'Lead Guitar' goes to Google with your click: exactly what the site promises never to send.
items.whats_wrong: Section 5 promises that text from the file cannot reach Google, because every field is typed. TypeScript checks extra keys only on an object written inside the call. An object built first, spread in or returned by a helper can carry an extra key, such as a track name, and track() as specified forwards the whole object to Google. The privacy end-to-end case opens a file but presses no mixer control, so it would not catch this.

before.text:
- **`track(name, fields)`** sends `gtag('event', name, fields)` once started, and nothing before —
  no console warning, unlike `sendGAEvent`.
- `track()`: nothing before the start; `['event', name, fields]` after it.

after.text:
- **`track(name, fields)`** calls `gtag('event', name, …)` once started, and nothing before — no
  console warning, unlike `sendGAEvent`. It sends only the fields its event declares, copied by name
  from a key list beside `AnalyticsEvents` that `typecheck` checks against it. An object built
  elsewhere with an extra key, such as a track name, therefore sends nothing more.

- `track()`: nothing before the start; `['event', name, fields]` after it, without any key the event
  does not declare.

items.proposed_fix: track() copies only the keys its event declares, from a per-event key list kept beside AnalyticsEvents. tsc checks each list against the interface both ways (no declared field missing, no unknown key). The track() unit test checks that an extra key is not sent.
items.why_it_works: The promise no longer depends on how each call site writes its object: whatever object arrives, only declared, typed fields leave. The cost is one short key list for each of the eleven events our code sends and about ten lines in track.ts, and the type check stops the lists drifting away from the interface.

plain_terms.excess-property check: TypeScript's error for a key the type does not declare; it runs only on an object written directly inside the call
plain_terms.spread: copying all keys of one object into another, written ...object
plain_terms.key list: a fixed list of the field names one event may send

severity_check.why: Today's call sites will likely pass objects written inside the call, so nothing leaks at launch; the risk is a later change. Cheap to close.

quotes.quote: Sentry's scrub already cuts their `?`, so this removes noise, not
Errors thrown inside Google's script are not ours:

items.central_claim_check: The two bullets exist (lines 298-302), and the first one calls itself noise removal. The Sentry spec (PR #191) confirms that its scrub already cuts fetch and xhr breadcrumb addresses at the first ? or # (its line 387 and lines 423-425). The same spec's setup creates one issue alert that emails leocaseiro for each new kind of error (its lines 564-569), and its interim health number is the share of visits that ended without an unhandled error (its lines 24-27). So an error from gtag.js that reached Sentry would open an issue, send one email and lower that number. Two details narrow the second bullet further. (1) gtag.js comes from another site. If the loader adds it without a crossorigin attribute, as Google's usual snippet does, the browser reports the script's own errors only as 'Script error.', and Sentry's default filter already drops that message (Sentry's eventFilters source, https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-javascript/blob/develop/packages/core/src/integrations/eventFilters.ts). denyUrls then matters only for an error with a real stack whose newest frame is in gtag.js, for example one thrown while our own code calls into it (reasoned, untested). (2) Whether gtag.js sends its hits with fetch or xhr, which Sentry records as breadcrumbs, or with navigator.sendBeacon, which it does not record, was not checked (untested); if it is sendBeacon, the first bullet has almost nothing to drop.
items.contradicts: none — checked section 6's other bullets, section 4 'Addresses' (Sentry cuts addresses at ? on purpose), the Non-goals, section 10 and 'Known limits'. Nothing else in the spec refers to the Google host list or to denyUrls.

spike.why: Needs Sentry 11 and Google's real script running together; neither is installed on this branch, because the Sentry code is not merged. The After text was applied to a scratch copy of the spec together with Group C's other Afters; the repo's own Prettier (print width 100), markdownlint-cli2 and cspell all pass on it.

items.scenario: Google's script throws an error on a visitor's phone in Sydney. With the spec as written, Sentry ignores it and you never hear of it. Without the two filters, you get one email from Sentry about an error inside Google's code, and that visit counts as a broken one in the health number. Error reports also show a few lines about Google's network calls, with their addresses already cut short.
items.whats_wrong: Section 6 adds two Google-specific filters to Sentry's settings, which are not merged yet: one drops Google's network calls from the error trail, the other ignores errors thrown inside Google's script. By the spec's own words the first removes only noise. Each is a small change to make later, if the noise ever appears, while adding them now widens this ticket's edits to NH-124's settings and adds a list of Google addresses to keep up to date.

  `www.google.com/ccm`. Sentry's scrub already cuts their `?`, so this removes noise, not

- **Errors thrown inside Google's script are not ours:** `denyUrls: [/googletagmanager\.com/]`.

  thrown inside Google's script. A `beforeBreadcrumb` host drop or a `denyUrls` entry is added only
  if either appears as noise in Sentry.

items.proposed_fix: Remove the two bullets from section 6 and add one Non-goals item: Sentry keeps Google's fetch and xhr breadcrumbs and any error thrown inside Google's script, and a filter is added only if either appears as noise in Sentry.
items.why_it_works: It keeps this ticket's changes to NH-124's Sentry setup to what the privacy choice needs, and removes a list of Google addresses nobody has to maintain yet. It costs little that anyone would see: the breadcrumbs are already cut at ?, and an error inside Google's script is rare, mostly filtered already, and would arrive as one email.

plain_terms.breadcrumb: a short note about an earlier event (a click, a network call) that travels inside the next error report
plain_terms.beforeBreadcrumb: Sentry's hook that can drop a breadcrumb before it is kept
plain_terms.denyUrls: a Sentry setting that ignores errors whose code comes from the listed addresses
plain_terms.NH-124: the Sentry error-monitoring ticket; its spec is on PR #191, not merged yet
plain_terms.health number: Sentry Release Health's share of visits that ended without an unhandled error, the interim health number in the Sentry spec
plain_terms.S4: decision S4 in the Sentry spec: Release Health on, as the interim health number

items.central_claim_check: web/app/layout.tsx:15-27 renders the page and then the Toaster inside <body>. client/src/components/ui/Sonner/Sonner.tsx:198-201 says the Toaster mounts last in the root layout, so plain Tab reaches a close button only after every page control, which is why it keeps the Alt+T hotkey. web/e2e/a11y.e2e.ts:270 sets the floor for /play at 12 controls; that counts controls with a hit area, close to, but not exactly, the number of Tab stops. Section 3 gives the card three answer buttons and Details: four Tab stops, five with Details open (its link). web/ has no skip link. The GOV.UK Design System places its cookie banner right after the opening body tag, before the skip link (https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/cookie-banner/); its banner sits in the page flow at the top, not floating, so it guides the order only. Last, as the Toaster is: they pass a dozen or more controls first, which is the reason Sonner.tsx gave the Toaster an Alt+T hotkey. The plan has to pick one and test it.
